stories.title: Cyclone ‘Akvan’ heads for Odisha; over one lakh people evacuated
stories.summary: Odisha Government closes coastal tourist sites including Chilika Lake, Puri beaches, Bhitarakanika and Nandankanan Zoological Park
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Odisha on Thursday (November 19, 2026) stepped up evacuation of people, positioning of disaster response forces and emptying of reservoirs in southern and coastal districts as the Severe Cyclonic Storm ‘Akvan’ is expected cross the State’s coast, close to east of Gopalpur, by noon of November 20.
Office of Special Relief Commissioner said more than one lakh people, including close to 10,000 pregnant women, have been shifted to safer places.
While Ganjam district under which Gopalpur lies alone has shifted over 50,000 people, Gajapati and Kandhamal districts have relocated 16,000 and 3000 people respectively.
Ghat roads (hill passes) such as Kalinga and Gajalbadi connecting Ganjam and Kandhamal districts have been barricaded, apprehending landslides.

“The Severe Cyclonic Storm “Akvan” over the westcentral Bay of Bengal moved northwards with the speed of 15 kmph during past six hours and lay centered about 420 km east-southeast of Narsapur (Andhra Pradesh), 400 km south-southeast of Kalingapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), 490 km south of Gopalpur (Odisha) and 550 km south of Puri (Odisha) and 590 km east-northeast of Chennai (Tamil Nadu),” the India Meteorological Department announced in a bulletin.

The IMD bulletin said it is likely to move north-northwestward and cross North Andhra Pradesh and Yanam and South Odisha coasts between Narsapur and Puri, close to east of Gopalpur, by noon of November 20, 2026, with maximum sustained wind speed of 90-100 kmph gusting to 110 kmph.
Experts, however, said the windspeed could come down to 70 to 80 km per hour when the cyclone would cross the coast.
A red warning for heavy to very heavy rainfall has been issued for Kendrapada, Jagatsinghpur, Puri, Ganjam, Gajapati, and Kandhamal districts.
Gopalpur Port authorities have secured machineries and ships in view advancing cyclone after the government’s warning.
“Water resources department has started depleting reservoirs in districts to be affected by the cyclone.
Engineers are continuously monitoring situation while technical teams have been deployed.
Two gates of major dam and 23 gates of different medium irrigation dams are kept opened,” said Odisha Chief Secretary Anu Garg.

stories.title: Cyclone Akvan Update: 39 trains cancelled, including Vande Bharat; 28 others affected – full list

article_sentences: Cyclone Akvan train cancellation list: The Ministry of Railways has cancelled 39 train services as a precautionary measure due to Cyclone Akvan.

In its latest bulletin, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said Cyclone Akvan is expected to make landfall between Narsapur in Andhra Pradesh and Puri in Odisha, near Gopalpur, with maximum sustained wind speeds of 90-100 kmph and gusts reaching 110 kmph.
Strong winds are expected along the south and north Odisha coasts as the cyclone approaches, it added.

“With Cyclone Akvan approaching the Odisha coast, 39 train services scheduled to operate on November 19, 20 and 21, 2026, have been cancelled as a precautionary measure to ensure passenger safety and minimise operational risks during the cyclone.
The cancellations cover several long-distance express, Vande Bharat, passenger and MEMU services connecting Odisha with neighbouring states.
A number of trains operating to and from Puri, Bhubaneswar, Cuttack and Brahmapur have been affected,” the ECoR said.

Among the cancelled services are the Bhubaneswar-Visakhapatnam Vande Bharat Express (20841/20842), Howrah-Puri Vande Bharat Express (22895/22896), Tatanagar-Brahmapur Vande Bharat Express (20891/20892) and Puri-Yesvantpur Garib Rath Express (22883/22884).
“Passengers are advised to take note of the cancellation of these train services and plan their journeys accordingly.

Passengers are advised to check the latest train timings and other details through the National Train Enquiry System (NTES) or other official railway enquiry channels before commencing their journey,” the zonal railway said.
Speaking to Indianexpress.com, a senior ECoR official said that apart from the cancelled trains, around 28 other trains have been rescheduled or regulated.

stories.headline: Delhi High Court Seeks Response Of ED, SFIO On Tina Ambani's Plea Seeking Disclosure Of LOC
stories.title: Delhi High Court Seeks Response Of ED, SFIO On Tina Ambani's Plea Seeking Disclosure Of LOC
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Delhi High Court on Thursday issued notice on a plea filed by Tina.

A. Ambani, wife of industrialist Anil Ambani, seeking disclosure of whether any Look-Out Circular (LOC) has been issued against her by investigating agencies, including the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) and the Enforcement Directorate (ED).
Justice Mini Pushkarna sought response of Bureau of Immigration, ED and SFIO while listing the matter on December 08.
Ambani has also sought suspension of any such LOC, if issued against her, to enable her to travel to Thailand, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Bhutan between December 10 and December 30.

She has sought directions to the Bureau of Immigration and the investigating agencies to disclose the existence and particulars of any LOC against her, including its copy, the originating agency, the case or proceeding in which it was opened, the date of issuance, reference number, grounds recorded and present status.

Advocate Arshdeep Singh Khurana appearing for Ambani submitted that she wants to travel abroad to visit her family and friends and therefore, wants to know if any travel restrictions have been imposed against her.
He said that though the two agencies had summoned her, there are no pending summons as of now and that she has not been called any further.
“I wish to travel from December 10 to visit my family.
This is a disclosure petition that if there is an LOC, they may tell me and if there is no LOC, then it may come on record,” he said.
Appearing for ED, Senior Advocate Zoheb Hossain said that two summons were issued to Ambani however she did not appear in response to either of them.

As he sought time to file a short response to the plea, Khurana told Court that Ambani had communicated to the agency her willingness to appear but was suffering from a spinal fracture at the relevant time.
He said that after her intimation, no further summons have been issued to her.

stories.title: Airtel takes top spot, HDFC loses brand crown

He succeeds retired Justice Ashok Bhushan, whose tenure as a chairperson ended on July 4, 2026. Following Justice Bhushan’s retirement, Justice Yogesh Khanna had been acting as the officiating chairperson of the Tribunal, Bar and Bench reported. A law graduate from Kurukshetra University, Justice Bindal began his law practice at the Punjab and Haryana High Court in September 1985. He was appointed as an Additional Judge of the High Court of Punjab & Haryana in March 2006. He was subsequently transferred to the Jammu and Kashmir High Court, where he assumed office on November 19, 2018, and was appointed Acting Chief Justice of the common High Court for Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh in December 2020. He was later appointed Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court and the Allahabad High Court before being elevated to the Supreme Court on February 13, 2023. He retired as a judge of the apex court on April 15, 2026.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Tuesday (November 17) rejected plea filed by the Uttar Pradesh government and Uttar Pradesh Avas Evam Vikas Parishad (Housing Board) challenging an Allahabad High Court judgment that had set aside a demand of Rs 388 crore raised against real estate developer M/s Gaursons India Pvt.
A bench of Justice PS Narasimha and Justice Alok Aradhe upheld the High Court's decision to quash the Chief Secretary's June 2022 order and the consequential demand notice of September 2022.
The matter pertains to land of Gaursons' predecessors-in-interest, which the Housing Board acquired for its Vasundhara Scheme in Ghaziabad.

In 1995, the Supreme Court disposed of the Housing Board's appeal on a compromise under which the acquired land (12.047 acres) would be adjusted in the scheme, to be used for water purification-related construction with the rest kept open, and no party would pay any value or compensation for the exchange.
In a 2004 Exchange Deed, two parcels (Khasra Nos. 948 and 1454) in Arthala village were allotted to the predecessors-in-interest which were sold to Gaursons in 2005.
It later emerged that the land had already been resumed by the District Magistrate in 1994 for a bird sanctuary.
After years of litigation, the Housing Board executed a second Exchange Deed in 2016, giving Gaursons alternative land in the Siddharth Vihar Yojana.
Gaursons had paid Rs 32.45 crore as land conversion charges.
It built 2,476 general houses and 450 EWS/LIG houses on the land, which were sold to homebuyers.

After a PIL in the High Court and a Special Investigation Team (SIT) report, the Chief Secretary's order of June 2022 directed that the land be allotted to Gaursons at the current bulk sale rate subsequent to which the Housing Board issued the Rs 388 crore demand notice.
The High Court set aside two conditions (ii & iii) of the order and the demand notice.
Thereafter, an appeal was filed before the Supreme Court.

stories.title: Amit Shah inaugurates key anti-terror conference; deliberations to focus on cross-border terrorism
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 19: Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Thursday inaugurated a two-day key anti-terror conference, which will deliberate on "cross-border terrorism" besides the development of future-ready counter-terrorism strategies and the strengthening of institutional capacities to meet emerging national security challenges, among others. Held annually, the conference has steadily grown into a significant gathering of operational forces, agencies working in the field of counter-terrorism, and experts from the technical, legal and forensic domains. It offers the agencies/forces an opportunity to collectively examine matters that have bearing on national security and the threats arising from terrorism. In keeping with the 'whole of government approach', the conference places particular emphasis on fostering synergy among all stakeholders. It seeks to establish formal as well as informal channels that enable coordinated and concerted action against terrorism. The conference also aims at contributing substantive inputs towards the formulation of future policy, a statement issued by the Home Ministry has said. The conference sessions will address a range of subjects, including obtaining evidence from foreign jurisdictions, the application of digital forensics and data analysis in counter-terrorism investigations, and the effective management of trials, it said. Sessions will also cover countering radicalisation and emerging hybrid threats to national security. "Further sessions will examine the tools, techniques and case experiences involved in disrupting terror financing networks, as well as the development of future-ready counter-terrorism strategies and the strengthening of institutional capacities to meet emerging national security challenges," said the statement issued on Wednesday. The conference is being organised by the National Investigation Agency (NIA) as a part of a continued effort to bolster the nation's collective response to terrorism. stories.title: Old or new IIT? The big dilemma
stories.summary: For Gaurav Kukreja, merely getting into an Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) was not enough. When he began preparing for the Joint Entrance Examination (JEE), he desired a seat only in IIT-Bombay. “For me, getting into any IIT wasn’t the main goal. It feels absurd now, but any IIT apart from the top ones felt like a disappointment,” he says.However, as the examination approached, his expectations changed. “When I started preparing, the motivation was high, and I had a strong belief that I’ll end up at IIT-Bombay… slowly though I felt that any IIT would work,” he recalls.Kukreja secured an All India Rank of 5,721 in JEE Advanced. It meant he could get a seat in most IITs, barring IIT-Bombay. He shortlisted Delhi and Kanpur, and eventually chose the latter although the institute in the national capital ranked higher. “I did my research and found the Kanpur campus to be much better in terms of the size, beauty, infrastructure, and hostel and campus laws,” he says. “And I had a weird calling towards it.”What Kukreja went through is pretty much what thousands of students face after JEE Advanced: Which IIT, which branch and what kind of college experience should I choose?Also Read: Inside the IIT Dream: The Staggering Cost of Pressure and AmbitionBranch or Brand?After the JEE Advanced results are declared, aspirants weigh opening and closing ranks, branch preferences, placement records and campus facilities. The decision can oftentimes involve a trade-off. A preferred branch at a newer IIT against a less-preferred discipline at an older one.Pravin Tyagi, managing director, Pace IIT & Medical, a coaching institute with centres across India, who has spent 27 years advising students through the JEE process, says, “The most common questions after the results are about comparing old and new IITs, and deciding which branch to choose.” Students also inquire about placement cells, industry connections, internships, laboratories, faculty and entrepreneurship opportunities. Parents, on the other hand, ask about food, safety, distance from home, language and whether their child will adjust to campus life.Swati Pundkar, a chemistry teacher at a junior college in Mumbai, and whose daughter was admitted to IIT-Kharagpur this academic year, says she looked at the institute's reputation, the branch, the academic environment and the opportunities available after graduation. “Sending your child to another city means thinking about their sustenance and whether they will be able to adapt to a new environment. Ultimately, we wanted an institution where our child could grow academically and professionally and independently,” she says.Tyagi believes older IITs have an advantage in industry relationships, placement networks and alumni connections. But he does not believe newer institutions are being ignored. “The new IITs are not being overlooked. They are being judged, discussed, debated and rightly questioned,” he points out.In some cases, family background and long-term career plans also influence branch preferences. According to Tyagi, students from construction and chemical business families often choose civil and chemical engineering; others consider management, civil services or entrepreneurship. “I advise students to join the course or branch that is their area of interest, because when you like what you have to learn for four years, you will enjoy it, and put your heart into those courses,” he says.The final call though ultimately depends on which institute offers the branch the student wants. “My teaching experience made me conscious about the importance of choosing the right branch for my child over the institute. We did discuss placements and the popularity of certain branches, but I did not want her to choose a discipline simply because everyone else was opting for it. The interest had to be there… because that is what will sustain her through the course,” Pundkar says.Choosing the right IIT and a branch after securing a JEE rank can be an overwhelming decision for students and parents. With multiple options, conflicting advice and expectations about career prospects, students often find themselves confused. Therefore, after students get their JEE ranks, they go through a counselling round, which plays an important role in helping them make choices based on their interests, strengths and long-term aspirations instead of simply following popular trends.Professor Pratik Sen, dean of student affairs at IIT-Kanpur, believes counselling can bring information overload, peer pressure and anxiety around placements and branch preferences. He advises students to look beyond the popularity of a discipline. “Every core discipline holds value, not just computer science,” he says. “Without proper material, nothing can be produced, and without knowledge and expertise in chemistry, high-quality materials are not possible.”Sen recommends examining curriculum, faculty, research opportunities and interdisciplinary learning. “Established IITs may offer mature research ecosystems, experienced faculty and strong alumni networks,” he explains. Teamwork and intellectual curiosity on campus, he adds, help build careers beyond a placement.At many IITs, students are also given an opportunity to assess institutions before submitting their preferences. Professor Abhijit Kshirsagar, faculty member in the department of electrical, electronics and communication engineering at IIT-Dharwad, says IITs conduct open houses after JEE Advanced results, allowing students and parents to visit campuses, meet faculty and learn about the facilities and programmes.The branch versus institute decision depends on a student’s ambitions. Some see engineering as a route into entrepreneurship or management; others are particular about a subject. “Some students have told me that engineering is a stepping stone [to entrepreneurship] because they want to be entrepreneurs, founders or managers,” he says. “I recently met a student in 11th standard who is clear about robotics, so he wants mechanical or mechatronics or an allied branch.”For Parv Mor, a quantitative developer at Citadel Securities who studied computer science and engineering at IIT-Kanpur, the discipline was non-negotiable. IIT-Bombay’s computer science programme was his first choice, but he would have considered any of the five older IITs.He believes the quality of academic interactions and education can differ between institutions, partly because older IITs have a longer record of producing talent. Yet he cautions against treating reputation as a guarantee. “You can be in a top IIT, but if you are not putting in the effort and do not have the drive to learn, your outcome will not be good,” he says. “A majority of students who excel are those who are genuinely curious to learn and innovate.”Also Read: Engineers to founders: How IITs are fuelling the startup boom in IndiaThe Weight of LegacyFor a newer IIT, building reputation takes time. Take IIT-Dharwad, which was established in 2016, for instance. It has grown from a temporary campus with fewer than 100 students to nearly 1,500 in about a decade. Its programmes have expanded from three core engineering disciplines to include chemical and civil engineering, maths and computing, and postgraduate courses.“We are the third generation. One advantage is that we have the benefit of youth. The faculty are younger, the environment is slightly more dynamic and we are less entrenched,” Kshirsagar says. But expectations are high as well. “As a 10-year-old institute, we’re expected to live up to the standards of IIT-Bombay and Delhi, which have 60 to 65 years behind them,” he laments.He adds that the difference is not necessarily whether a laboratory or course exists. In power and energy, he believes IIT-Dharwad’s facilities are comparable in many respects with those at IIT-Bombay; inter-institute agreements also allow students to access facilities at other IITs. But an institution’s reputation is built over decades, through research, faculty, graduating batches and alumni networks.“In institution terms, 10 years is an extremely short time period. The older IITs enjoy a significant advantage in decades of alumni networks and established relations,” says Kshirsagar. A student who gets an internship at a company can help open the door for subsequent batches. “The first student to get in is the hardest. It builds up exponentially,” he adds.The merit of the chosen IIT is only realised in the later years of the degree, says Siddhesh Kadam, an IIT-Gandhinagar graduate from the 2026 batch. Not securing an internship can create a sense of desperation among students, particularly at newer IITs where placement records are still developing.“At IIT-Gandhinagar, I have seen students become anxious about whether they will find a job. I would not generalise this to all IITs, as older institutions have stronger placement records. Much also depends on market demand and how many people companies are looking to hire. But these uncertainties do affect how students experience their time on campus,” says Kadam, who is currently working as an engineer at Micron Technology.Kukreja, however, believes differences between IITs are more visible in the overall experience than in the fundamentals of education. “Culture, alumni network, prestige, infrastructure and international exposure are some of the things which are hard to replicate for newer IITs, since they take time to develop,” he says. He adds that the older IIT tag can carry weight during internships and research opportunities, as well as later in a career.Risha Agarwal, an IIT-Bombay civil engineering graduate now pursuing an MBA at Stanford, had a fixed preference. “When I was preparing for JEE, my dream college was IIT-Bombay. I didn’t want to go anywhere else,” she says. A campus visit for a scholarship interview only strengthened that belief.She also sees a difference between the five new IITs and the rest, particularly when it comes to placements, research ecosystems and alumni networks. “Because the older IITs are so old, they have a large alumni base, strong research potential and professionals who have been there for long. The newer IITs cannot replicate these strengths,” she says. However, she notes that several IITs outside the top group have strong research capabilities even if their placement opportunities differ.Expansion, but with gapsPlacement statistics are closely watched, but institutes report different measures and reporting periods.For 2024-25, IIT-Bombay reported 2,469 registered students out of which 2,040 participated in placements. It recorded 1,422 accepted offers, with an average cost to company (CTC) of Rs26.45 lakh and a median of Rs20 lakh. IIT-Kanpur said 1,225 of 1,530 registered students got placed by May 2025. IIT-Dharwad recorded 123 placements from 147 registered students, with an average CTC of Rs14.65 lakh and a median of Rs12.18 lakh. The data has been collected from media reports and institution websites.For Agarwal, recruitment remains a key differentiator. “There is definitely a lot of difference between the top three or top five IITs and the others, mostly in terms of placements because a lot of companies that come to the top five IITs do not go to other IITs,” she says. But she points out that research and core academic programmes can be strong at institutions that attract fewer recruiters.The government is also stepping up with continuous budget allocations to strengthen the IIT network in India, with reportedly more work done at the new IITs.The Union Budget for 2026-27 allocated Rs12,123 crore to the IITs collectively, compared with Rs11,349 crore in the 2025-26 Budget Estimates, an increase of about 6.8 percent. The headline allocation is for the system as a whole; it does not divide older and newer institutions.In May 2025, the Union Cabinet approved Rs11,828.79 crore for expansion at five newer IITs—Tirupati, Palakkad, Bhilai, Jammu and Dharwad—over 2025-26 to 2028-29. The plan is expected to add capacity for more than 6,500 students and includes research parks.But the expansion of the IIT system is not only about how many institutions it has, how many students it can accommodate or the opportunities it can offer. Gender representation, in that sense, is another measure of how the system is changing. According to the Joint Implementation Committee's JEE (Advanced) 2025 Report, women accounted for 3,664 of the 18,188 seats allotted across all the IITs in 2025, or 20.15 percent. The report's institute-wise data shows that the proportion ranged from 19.19 percent at IIT-Kharagpur to 21.57 percent at IIT-Tirupati.As the IIT network grows, there is definitely an increase in the number of seats and institutions, but questions of access and representation remain part of the conversation. For students choosing these institutes, the experience is not measured only by rankings, placement packages or the number of companies that visit.The question is also no longer simply which institution carries the oldest or strongest legacy. It is what each campus can offer its students, how those opportunities are distributed, and how quickly newer institutions can build the ecosystems that students have come to associate with the IIT brand name.
